In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no Cretaceous leaf mining insect survived the K-Pg event and that the high diversity of damage on the Mexican Hat flora was caused by an influx of novel leaf miners during the Paleocene.
the insect fauna of Mexican Hat is a Paleocene fauna, and the leaf miners of Mexican Hat are Paleocene leaf miners, not Cretaceous survivors.
the high insect damage at Mexican Hat is the result of the arrival of new insect herbivores, not the result of survivorship of insect herbivores from Cretaceous refugia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Mexican Hat site exhibits the highest damage diversity known from the early Paleocene and the lowest plant diversity, and that the high damage diversity is related to a transient influx of novel insect taxa.
, in the early Paleocene Great Plains, the demise of Cretaceous leaf-mining insects and the arrival of novel leaf-mining insects occurred within the same time interval.

the Cretaceous insect leaf miners were not able to survive the K-Pg event, but the novel Paleocene leaf miners were able to survive the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) and are still around today.
The main takeaway from our work is that
insect herbivores can be highly host specific and that the loss of insect-feeding diversity at the K-Pg transition is not a simple reflection of the loss of host diversity.

the early Paleocene insect herbivore fauna of North America was novel, not just in its diversity but in its feeding habits, which may have been a major factor in the low diversity of the early Paleocene flora.
, despite the high diversity of leaf mines at Mexican Hat, the insect fauna was not yet diverse enough to cause the same level of damage as in the Cretaceous.
